solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Scot bared bottom by road? That's most gross!

indicators.note: bared means stripped, so the word Scot loses its outer letters

parts.note: arse is British slang for the backside
ST is the abbreviation for street, a road

explanation.surface: A kilted Scotsman mooning beside the highway — about as vulgar as it gets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bared' strips the outside letters from SCOT, leaving CO. ARSE is the British word for a bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse means vulgar or crude, a near synonym of gross, and this is its superlative.

clue.text: 50% off price to acquire banger, it being this?

definitions.text: 50% off price to acquire banger, it being this?

indicators.note: to acquire is to take in, so one piece goes inside the other
taking fifty per cent off a word leaves only its first half

parts.note: cost is a price
a banger and a heap are both slang for a decrepit old car

explanation.surface: Buying a clapped-out car at half price is, of course, a bargain-basement move.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of COST is CO, which takes in HEAP. A banger is British slang for an old rattletrap car; the whole clue also describes such a purchase.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapo describes something bought for very little, as an old wreck of a car bought at half price would be.

clue.text: Smitten, I dream about Romeo?

indicators.note: about means around, so the shuffled letters go round the Romeo letter
smitten means struck hard, so the letters of I dream are knocked into a new order

parts.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A lovestruck girl confesses that her dreams are all of Romeo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smitten' turns I DREAM into ADMIER, and 'about' places R inside. Read whole, the clue is what a besotted fan of Romeo might say.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone infatuated, who daydreams of a beloved, is a devotee or fan of that person.

clue.text: Small children returning can finally pay attention — it's time to learn

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: returning means the word for can is read backwards

parts.note: can is slang for a lavatory, a loo

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word pay

parts.note: to give an ear is to give attention

explanation.surface: Little ones coming back from the toilet can at last listen — lessons are starting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns LOO (can, slang for toilet) into OOL; 'finally' takes Y from pay.
explanation.definitionFit: An academic session in which pupils are taught runs for a twelve-month cycle, a learning period.

clue.text: Go away, having exhausted urges for some food

parts.note: scram is a brusque order to go away
bled means drained or exhausted, as of funds
to egg on is to urge

explanation.surface: Someone told to clear off after running out of urges, as in a rebuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'urges' is a verb here, giving EGGS as in egging someone on.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaten eggs stirred in a pan are a common breakfast dish, an example of food.

clue.text: One African country or another that's good for Zulu

indicators.note: good for Zulu says one letter stands in place of the other between the two country names

parts.note: another African country, the Gambia, is the starting word
Zulu is Z in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A geography quiz note that one African nation becomes another if you swap a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: GAMBIA has G (good) where the answer has Z (Zulu); 'Zulu' also seems to belong to the African scene.
explanation.definitionFit: This landlocked southern African republic, once Northern Rhodesia, is a nation of that continent.

clue.text: Assistant's preposterous plan

indicators.note: preposterous literally means back in front, so the last letter of the plan word comes round to the front

parts.note: an idea is a plan

explanation.surface: A helper's scheme is dismissed as absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'preposterous' is used in its Latin sense, 'behind-before': IDEA has its end letter A moved to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A helper or aide-de-camp is an assistant to someone senior.

clue.text: Run after black bag

indicators.note: after places the run word behind the letter for black

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a run in tights or stockings is a ladder

explanation.surface: Someone sprints after a black bag snatched in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' is a noun here, the British LADDER in stockings, not a sprint.
explanation.definitionFit: The organ that stores urine is a sac or bag; footballs also have an inner one.

clue.text: For one worker, single currency lacks European element

parts.note: the ant is a classic example of a worker
I, the Roman numeral, is one

indicators.note: lacks says the currency word is missing a letter

parts.note: money is currency

explanation.surface: The euro, a single currency, seen from one worker's point of view, minus Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'single currency' looks like the euro, but splits into I and MONEY, which 'lacks' E.
explanation.definitionFit: Antimony is a metalloid chemical element, symbol Sb, number 51.

clue.text: Position of leadership abandoned by Henry Wood

indicators.note: abandoned by says the leadership word loses the letter for Henry

parts.note: to be at the helm is to be in charge
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A leadership role is given up by Sir Henry Wood, the conductor who founded the Proms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry Wood' reads as the conductor's name, but Henry is H and Wood is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The timber of this broadleaved tree is a wood used for furniture and coffins.

clue.text: Strict dad hasn't right to go ape about nothing

indicators.note: about means around, so the anagram goes around the nothing word
to go ape is to go wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: FA, short for sweet Fanny Adams, is British slang for nothing

explanation.surface: A stern father who isn't allowed to fly off the handle over trifles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go ape' scrambles DAD HASNT plus R into HARDANDST, and 'about' wraps that round FA, short for 'sweet Fanny Adams', British slang for nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Rules that are fixed and cannot be bent are rigid, inflexible and so strict.

clue.text: Essential quality of e.g. Bomber Harris is new to conflict

indicators.note: conflict means struggle or clash, so the letters of the fodder are set at odds and rearranged

explanation.surface: Sir Arthur 'Bomber' Harris, chief of RAF Bomber Command, new to war, has an essential quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bomber Harris' looks like one name, but Bomber belongs to the definition (a bomber aircraft) and Harris starts the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomber aircraft must be fit to fly, the essential property of any plane.

clue.text: They play an old song at the start

parts.note: per means a or an, as in ten pounds per head
former means old or one-time

indicators.note: at the start picks the first letter of the word song

explanation.surface: Musicians playing an old song to open their set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an' gives PER, as in 'so much an hour'.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors and musicians on stage play roles or instruments, so they are those who play.

clue.text: Faith possibly shown by a mother

parts.note: a dam is the mother of an animal, especially a horse

explanation.surface: Religious faith as shown in a mother.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam Faith was a British pop singer and actor of the 1960s, so 'Faith' is his surname, with 'possibly' marking an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The singer Adam Faith shares the first name, so his surname can point to the first man's name.

clue.text: Sporting event held in Irish town mostly

parts.note: pent in means held in or confined

indicators.note: mostly says the town's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Athlone is a town in the Irish midlands

explanation.surface: A sports fixture staged largely in a town in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held in' looks like a container signal but is PENT, as in pent in.
explanation.definitionFit: This contest of five events, such as the modern Olympic one, is a sporting competition.

clue.text: Billy Graham keeps backing Scottish region

indicators.note: backing means the held letters are read backwards
keeps says the name Billy Graham holds the letters within it

explanation.surface: The American evangelist Billy Graham is a supporter of a Scottish district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' and 'backing' hide the region backwards in 'Billy Graham'.
explanation.definitionFit: Argyll is a historic county on Scotland's west coast, an area of that country.

clue.text: Contributions from bowler and batsman take too long

parts.note: in cricket a bowler delivers an over of six balls
a batsman scores a run

explanation.surface: A cricket match drags on thanks to the bowler and batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an OVER is a set of six balls bowled, and a RUN is what the batsman scores.
explanation.definitionFit: To go beyond the allotted time is to exceed it, as a meeting may.

clue.text: Love, it's bang out of order showing off

indicators.note: out of order means the letters are not in their proper sequence

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A lover objects that a brag about sex is out of line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' gives O, the zero score in tennis, which joins ITS BANG in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Bragging about one's achievements is a form of vaunting or flaunting oneself.

clue.text: Casual worker from France getting precedence

indicators.note: getting precedence means the from and France pieces come before the worker

parts.note: of can mean from, as in a man of Kent
F is the international vehicle code for France
a hand is a worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A French temp gets priority over the others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casual worker' wants to be the definition, a temp; but 'worker' is only part of the wordplay, and 'Casual' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An unconcerned, curt or nonchalant manner is casual and careless.

clue.text: A long way back, acquiring recipe for hotchpotch

indicators.note: acquiring means taking in, so the recipe letter goes inside

parts.note: far means a long way
ago means back in time
R stands for recipe, Latin for take, on prescriptions

explanation.surface: Long ago someone picked up a recipe for a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recipe' gives R, from the Latin 'take' written on old prescriptions; 'hotchpotch' is also a stew, fitting the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrago is a confused jumble or medley, the same as a hotchpotch.

clue.text: Red giant enthrals institute

indicators.note: enthrals means holds captive, so the giant word encloses the letter

parts.note: a titan is a giant

explanation.surface: A red giant star captivates a scientific institute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red giant' reads as a star, but splits into definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian painter's favourite shade of auburn hair gave its name to a bright reddish-brown colour.

clue.text: A right Charlie's held in honour

indicators.note: held in means the Charlie letter is enclosed by the other pieces

parts.note: a claim is a right or entitlement
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A real fool is held in honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' is British slang for a fool, but here is C, placed inside A CLAIM.
explanation.definitionFit: To acclaim is to praise publicly, which is to honour.

clue.text: Hydrocarbon could be one if left out

definitions.note: could be marks the answer as one example of a hydrocarbon, a compound of carbon and hydrogen

indicators.note: out means disordered, so the letters of one if and the left letter are rearranged

explanation.surface: A chemist's note that one hydrocarbon might form if something were omitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left out' looks like omission; L (left) joins ONE IF and 'out' mixes them. 'could be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An olefin, or alkene, is an unsaturated compound of hydrogen and carbon with a double bond.

clue.text: Asian garment is worn by academician from the east

indicators.note: from the east means read from right to left in an across answer
worn by means the academician wears the is word round him

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician

explanation.surface: An Eastern dress is worn by a member of the Royal Academy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worn by' makes the academician the wearer, so IS goes outside him; 'from the east' then reads the result right to left, IRAS turning round.
explanation.definitionFit: The sari is a long draped cloth worn by women in India and South Asia.

clue.text: Selfish git heading off essential social reforms

indicators.note: reforms means forms again, so the letters are arranged anew

parts.note: git as written, with the heading of essential, its first letter E, set beside it

explanation.surface: A self-centred oaf cuts off necessary social reforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' looks like removal but gives E, the head of 'essential'; 'reforms' then mixes GIT, E and SOCIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: An egoistical person is self-absorbed and puts themselves first, the meaning of selfish.

clue.text: After turnover, energy corporation is silent

indicators.note: after a turnover the energy and corporation pieces are read upside down in this down answer

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy
corporation is old British slang for a pot belly, a tum

explanation.surface: An energy company says nothing after its turnover figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turnover' and 'corporation' are business words; here corporation is an old joke word for a big belly, TUM, and 'After turnover' flips E plus TUM to give MUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mute means unable or unwilling to speak, so making no sound.

clue.text: Briefly, where to find something to eat in a Brazil?

definitions.text: where to find something to eat in a Brazil?
definitions.meaning: a Brazil is a nut, whose edible kernel is within a hard case

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in summary, and literally where a kernel sits inside a nut's case.

clue.text: Chap bailiff periodically visited

indicators.note: periodically picks every other letter of the word bailiff

explanation.surface: A man the bailiff called on from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'periodically' takes the even letters of bAiLiFf.
explanation.definitionFit: Alf is a short man's name, and crosswords use any man's name for chap.

clue.text: Term for threatening scowl

indicators.note: a term is an end or limit, so the term for threatening is its final letter

parts.note: to lower, or lour, is to frown or scowl

explanation.surface: A word meaning a menacing frown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Term for' looks like 'a word for' but means the end of 'threatening', G; LOWER is to frown, and the whole clue defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To stare angrily and menacingly is to frown in an intimidating way, a threatening look.

clue.text: When retiring, celebrity's not getting it all together

parts.note: as means when, as in as I was leaving

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the celebrity and not words are read backwards

parts.note: a celebrity is a big name
no can mean not, as in no better

explanation.surface: A shy celebrity is not joining in with everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' looks like shyness but reverses NAME and NO to give ONEMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes people acting in unison, with complete agreement.
